content: Between 2013 and 2015, national regulatory authorities in priority countries were assessed twice annually, with follow-up missions conducted to evaluate the implementation of institutional development plans. Technical assistance was provided to Member States planning to conduct Systematic Immunization Assessments (SIAs), and recommendations and plans were disseminated to WHO headquarters and other Member States. Two regional training sessions were held annually to facilitate the sharing of experiences in improving immunization information systems, with a focus on introducing electronic immunization registries. The impact of existing National Immunization Technical Advisory Groups (NITAGs) was assessed, and results were analyzed and disseminated by June 2014. Efforts were made to promote the establishment of NITAGs in 18 countries that lacked them, with site visits conducted in 2–4 Member States annually from 2013 to 2015. Guidance and best practice documents were published by June 2014. The Guide to Tailoring Immunization Programmes (TIP) was developed and implemented in two Member States per year during this period, with best practices documented by the end of 2014. Two articles on TIP and its application were submitted to peer-reviewed journals between 2014 and 2015. Case-based surveillance systems for measles and rubella were implemented to collect monthly data at the regional level from all Member States with established case-based reporting by the end of 2013. Regular epidemiological and virological reports were produced, including monthly WHO EpiData tables and quarterly WHO EpiBriefs, which were distributed via email and posted online. Technical assistance and timelines were developed to integrate rubella-related surveillance systems and reporting, with conference calls held with 2–4 Member States not yet reporting case-based rubella data from 2013 to 2015. At least 95% of national measles/rubella laboratories in the WHO Europe laboratory network maintained full accreditation annually during this period. Monthly Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS) reporting was implemented in coordination with the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) in 6–8 Member States by the end of 2014. Regional and Member State-specific IT tools (MRSM) were finalized and implemented in 4–6 Member States between 2013 and 2015. Efforts to integrate laboratory and epidemiological data included piloting systems in 2–4 Member States using unique identifiers between 2013 and 2014. A working group within the Vaccine-preventable Diseases and Immunization Programme (VPI) of the WHO Regional Office for Europe was established to address integration and consistent reporting, with a written plan completed by the end of 2013. The MRLDMS reporting system was implemented by the end of 2013. A manual on vaccine safety risk management was published in the first quarter of 2014, and three subregional training sessions on vaccine safety risk management were conducted at national and subnational levels in 2014 and 2015. Training packages for measles and rubella were developed and accredited by national authorities for continuing medical education by mid-2014. Regional guidelines on outbreak response were published by the end of 2013 to support the development of national measles/rubella outbreak response guidelines and action plans. Starting with the 2014 status reports, national outbreak response plans were included in the documentation process for verifying measles and rubella elimination. High-level advocacy visits to priority countries were conducted twice annually from 2013 to 2015. Roundtable meetings on measles and rubella elimination were held with 10–12 priority countries in November 2013 and November 2014. Two advocacy products were produced annually during this period to address specific challenges, opportunities, and topical issues. All 53 Member States participated in European Immunization Week (EIW) in 2014 and 2015. Measles and rubella messages were developed and disseminated prior to EIW each year, and a full EIW narrative report was published by July 15 annually. Two healthcare worker resource materials (job aids) were produced annually from 2013 to 2015 and made available online through the Regional Office’s Immunization Resource Centre. These materials were applied within healthcare worker communities and implemented in at least one Member State per year in 2014 and 2015. WHO EpiData and EpiBrief reports summarizing epidemiological and laboratory data on measles, rubella, polio, and other vaccine-preventable diseases were regularly produced and disseminated from 2013 to 2015. A bloggers for health strategy was formulated and shared with Member States by November 2013, followed by a bloggers for health forum in Copenhagen in the first half of 2014. At least two measles and rubella-related tweets, web articles, online news stories, or blogs were posted weekly from 2013 to 2015. French and German versions of the immunization reminder/tracker app for smartphones were launched by EIW 2014. Support was provided to at least one Member State annually to strengthen the immunization sections of their websites. A concept paper for a decision-making app was completed in 2013, with development initiated in 2014. Technical assistance on vaccine communications, including awareness campaigns, risk/crisis communication, behavioral communication training, and social mobilization support, was provided to three Member States annually from 2013 to 2015. Reports were produced for each country, outlining recommendations and outcomes of the support provided. Funding for revitalizing the MECACAR platform was secured by June 2014, and a cross-border coordination meeting between the European and Eastern Mediterranean regions was held by June 2014 to develop and endorse a Joint Measles and Rubella Activity Plan. Technical assistance visits were conducted in 3–5 Member States annually from September to December between 2013 and 2015. A report summarizing outcomes of four intercountry meetings held in 2012–2013 was produced. Annual Regional Verification Commission meetings were followed by the publication of meeting reports within two months. An analysis of all reports submitted by Member States was reviewed and published by the end of the first quarter of the following year.
